lesson.subtitle: Lesson 16 -- It Was Decided
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Janderson Roberto Teixeira | Lesson 16 -- It Was Decided
lesson.grammar_point: present simple and past simple passive

listenings.text: Read any business headline and you will notice something strange. Rates were raised. Jobs were cut. A new director was appointed. Nobody seems to do anything, and things simply happen. That is the passive, and journalists use it for a simple reason: in the news, what happened is more interesting than who did it. Sometimes the person is not important. Sometimes everybody already knows who it was. And sometimes, honestly, nobody wants to say. When you do need the person, add by and the name, as in the deal was approved by the board. But most of the time you do not need it, and the sentence is cleaner without it. So the next time you explain a decision to a client, start with the decision, not with the people in the meeting.

Good morning, and here is the business news at eight. Harbor Capital and Northgate Bank are going to merge, it was announced this morning. The deal was approved by both boards on Thursday, and shareholders were told by letter last night. The new bank will be called Harbor Northgate, and its main office will stay in New York. A new chief executive was not named, and no decision about jobs was made. In other news, interest rates were raised again yesterday, for the third time this year. And the price of coffee was cut at two of the biggest chains in the country. That is all for now. More at nine.

extra_audio.text: Rachel asks Janderson if he has seen the headline about the merger. He asks her when it was announced. She tells him it was decided behind closed doors and that the shareholders were told last night. He asks if any of their clients were affected, and she says two of them are. Finally, he decides to call both clients before they read it in the news.

paras: Harbor Capital and Northgate Bank are going to merge. The news was announced at seven o'clock on Monday morning, and by eight it was the main headline on every financial website in the country.

The deal was not decided in a day. It was discussed behind closed doors for almost a year, and it was approved by both boards last Thursday. Shareholders were told by letter on Sunday night, a few hours before the public.

For clients, very little changes at first. Accounts are managed by the same teams, fees are kept at the same level for twelve months, and no new products are launched until the two systems are joined. A new chief executive is expected to be appointed in the spring.

What is not in the announcement is just as interesting. Nobody says who started the conversation, or which bank needed the other more. In news like this, the passive is not only grammar. It is a way of telling you what happened without telling you who did it.
